proposals.after: Therefore commanders like Yi Yin and Lü Shang had descendants with states, standing alongside Shang and Zhou.

proposals.before: Classical Zhou jurisprudence included multi-layered evidentiary and mitigation frameworks.
proposals.after: Zhou offices had the methods of the Five Hearings, Eight Deliberations, Three Inquiries, Three Pardons, and Three Exemptions.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic version omits the named Zhou legal categories present in the Chinese and literal fields.

proposals.before: Set this in statute: those over eighty, below eight, and pregnant women before weaning, as well as teachers and dwarf retainers who should be arrested, are to be held by summons rather than bound detention.'
proposals.after: Set this in statute: those over eighty, below eight, and pregnant women who have not yet given birth, as well as music masters and dwarfs who should be arrested, are to be held by summons rather than bound detention.'
proposals.reason: 未乳 means not yet having given birth, not 'before weaning'; 師 here are music masters.

proposals.before: Across the mid- and late Western Han reigns, capital sentences still averaged about one execution per thousand-odd persons yearly, and severe non-capital punishments ran at more than triple that rate.
proposals.after: Now Han's way has flourished for over two hundred years; examining the six reigns from Zhao, Xuan, Yuan, Cheng, Ai, and Ping, capital judgments averaged about one death sentence for every thousand-odd persons per year, while punishments from exile up to right-foot amputation were more than triple that rate.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic paraphrase omits the six named emperors (昭、宣、元、成、哀、平) that the Chinese enumerates.

proposals.before: In early Eastern Han recovery, social conditions resembled early Han: pro-weak governance and reduced private coercive power.
proposals.after: Since Jianwu and Yongping, people had newly escaped war calamities and cherished life, as between Gaozu and Hui; governance suppressed the strong and supported the weak, the court lacked ministers wielding private awe and favor, and localities lacked heroic magnates.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic paraphrase omits the named comparison to Gaozu and Hui (高、惠) present in the Chinese.

proposals.before: Per capita criminal adjudication fell dramatically versus late Western Han, indicating relative legal clarity.
proposals.after: By per-capita calculation, adjudicated prison cases were less than two-tenths of the Cheng–Ai interval, and may be called clear.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic paraphrase omits the named Cheng and Ai interval (成、哀之間).

proposals.before: He reinterprets historical shifts as responses to declining social-moral conditions.
proposals.after: Xunzi having said this, further arguing from common opinion: Yu inherited after Yao and Shun and, because his virtue had declined, made corporal punishments; Tang and Wu followed because customs were thinner than in the age of Tang-Yu.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic paraphrase omits the named rulers 禹、堯舜、湯武、唐虞 present in the Chinese.

proposals.before: Given post-Zhou/Qin social deterioration, applying ultra-lenient antiquarian models is seen as impractical and dangerous.
proposals.after: Now Han inherits the exhausted flow of declining Zhou and violent Qin; customs are already thinner than the Three Dynasties, yet practicing Yao-Shun punishments is like controlling a fierce horse with light tack—contrary to timely rescue.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic paraphrase omits Yao-Shun (堯舜) and the Zhou/Qin framing present in the Chinese.

proposals.before: Set this in statute: those over eighty years old, those under eight, pregnant women who have not yet given birth, and masters or dwarfs who should be arrested and detained are to be detained by summons rather than kept in bonds.'
proposals.after: Set this in statute: those over eighty, those under eight, pregnant women who have not yet given birth, music masters, and dwarfs who must be arrested and detained shall be held under summons rather than in bonds.'
proposals.reason: 師 in this legal list means music masters; the revision also removes repetition and matches the literal field.

proposals.before: Now Han's way had reached flourishing for over two hundred years; examining the six reigns from Zhao, Xuan, Yuan, Cheng, Ai, and Ping, capital judgments averaged about one death sentence for every thousand-odd persons per year, while punishments from exile up to right-foot amputation were more than triple that rate.
proposals.after: The Han way had now flourished for more than two hundred years. Examining the six reigns of Zhao, Xuan, Yuan, Cheng, Ai, and Ping, capital cases ending in death averaged a little more than one person in every thousand each year; punishments from shaving the beard through amputation of the right foot were more than three times as numerous.
proposals.reason: 耐 is a shaving punishment, not exile; the revision also clarifies the six-reign comparison.

proposals.before: Xunzi having said this, further arguing from common opinion: Yu inherited after Yao-Shun and because his virtue had declined made corporal punishments; Tang and Wu followed because customs were thinner than Tang-Yu.
proposals.after: Xunzi's words being so, he further reasoned from the conventional account: Yu succeeded Yao and Shun, but believing virtue had declined, instituted mutilating punishments; Tang and Wu continued them because customs were less refined than in the age of Yao and Shun.
proposals.reason: The revision restores the argument's subjects and chronology in grammatical English.

proposals.before: Now Han inherits the exhausted flow of declining Zhou and violent Qin; customs are already thinner than Three Dynasties, yet practicing Yao-Shun punishments is like controlling a fierce horse with light tack-contrary to timely rescue.
proposals.after: Now Han inherits the utter exhaustion left by declining Zhou and violent Qin. Customs are already less refined than under the Three Dynasties, yet applying the punishments of Yao and Shun is like controlling a fierce, bolting horse with a light bridle, contrary to what the times require.
proposals.reason: The revision preserves every historical comparison and renders the light-bridle analogy in grammatical English.

decisions.after: Thus, when Yi Yin and Lü Shang served as commanders, their descendants received states that endured alongside Shang and Zhou.
decisions.reason: 伊、呂 names Yi Yin and Lü Shang, while 之將 places them in the military-command context of the passage; the original paraphrase omitted both men and their descendants' states.

decisions.after: From the Jianwu through Yongping eras, the people had only recently emerged from the disasters of war and were mindful of preserving life, as in the time of Emperor Gaozu and Emperor Hui. Government policy restrained the strong and supported the weak; at court no minister privately wielded the power to inspire fear or grant favors, and in the localities there were no domineering magnates.
decisions.reason: The Chinese compares Jianwu and Yongping conditions to the time of Gaozu and Emperor Hui and details the policy of restraining the strong, supporting the weak, and curbing private power; the revision restores those specifics in natural English.

decisions.after: On a per capita basis, adjudicated criminal cases were less than two-tenths as numerous as during the reigns of Emperor Cheng and Emperor Ai; the administration could be called clear.
